I Did a Boudoir Shoot…Even Though I Was Terrified

By
Cassinda Scharff
-
July 31, 2026
0
Facebook
Pinterest
Linkedin
ReddIt
Email
    Telegram
    Copy URL

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 7:24
Instaread

I did a boudoir shoot, which is a sentence I never really thought I would say because, despite my willingness to share deeply personal information on the internet, the idea of standing mostly naked in front of a camera while someone tells me to arch my back until it might break felt like my own personal version of hell.

And yet, there I was. In lingerie… voluntarily. Trust me, I’m just as surprised as you are.

I wish I could tell you I walked into that room radiating confidence and that I had finally reached some magical stage of womanhood where I loved every inch of my body. That I had completely healed my relationship with my body and thought, You know what the world needs? Professional photographs of my ass. Newsflash: absolutely not.

I was nervous and painfully aware of every part of my body I have spent years criticizing. My stomach, my thighs, the weird freckles and birthmarks only I seem to recognize. The parts that have changed with age, babies, life, and the general audacity of gravity. Give a girl a break, dang.

I think I had this idea that I needed to feel confident before doing something like a boudoir shoot, like confidence was a prerequisite and I had somehow skipped the required course. Ask my photographer how many times I texted her saying, “Are we sure?”, “I’m nervous,” and, “What if they’re terrible?” (Shout out to Teagan Noelle Photography). And I’m sure no one is surprised that this was discussed multiple times in therapy.

I had this whole plan. I would lose weight first, maybe I would even tone something? Maybe I would finally figure out how to have the body I thought I was supposed to have after multiple pregnancies, and honestly, even before them. THEN I would feel ready, right??

The problem is that the goalpost always moves. I know I’m not the only one with this problem, too. There has always been something I could improve before I allowed myself to feel good. A number on the scale. A clothing size. A picture I didn’t like. Some new flaw I had apparently failed to notice until I caught myself at a terrible angle in Target’s dressing room lighting. Side note: seriously, who designed fitting-room lighting? Shit, y’all. That right there is an injustice.

Needless to say, I did not hit the goal that never stopped moving. Yeah, yeah. I know. Shocking.

So I didn’t walk into my boudoir shoot feeling ready. I just walked in.

You guys… I didn’t even get my hair and makeup done because I was so focused on everything else that I forgot to book it, and then it was too late. Don’t ask me if I hit up BlushTan Hudson before the shoot, because we know I didn’t (and it was a laaarge regret). The mistakes were really piling on here…

I quickly showered, doused myself in tanning lotion that I PRAYED wouldn’t blow up in my face, did my makeup, and literally ran out of time to do my hair. We’re lucky it was brushed, okay? And I kept waiting for some kind of transformation. I thought maybe I would look in the mirror and suddenly become an entirely different person. Someone sexy and confident who naturally knew what to do with her hands and face in pictures. (Hint: still no). But I did it anyway.

Somewhere between laughing at myself, trying to remember to point my toes, and realizing that posing for boudoir photos is apparently a full-body workout, something shifted. And I mean FULL BODY. Don’t say I didn’t warn you. I stopped analyzing myself quite so much. Not completely, because my brain is still my brain and she is nothing if not committed to the bit. But for a little while, I wasn’t mentally creating a list of everything I wanted to change. I wasn’t comparing myself to anyone else or immediately searching for the angle I liked least.

I was just… me. A woman. A wife. A mom. A person who has lived a whole lot of life in this body. This body has carried babies. It has experienced loss. It has run races, gotten stronger. It has kept moving during seasons when mentally, I didn’t feel capable of moving at all. And yet, I have spent years criticizing it. It’s me. Hi. I’m the problem, it’s me.

I don’t know when I learned to look at pictures of myself and immediately search for what was wrong, but I know I’m very good at it. I can look at a photo where everyone else sees a happy memory and somehow find the exact part of myself I wish looked different. It’s almost impressive… almost. Boudoir forced me to see myself through someone else’s lens. Literally, obviously, but also in a way I wasn’t expecting. The photographer wasn’t cataloging my perceived flaws. She was just photographing… me. And maybe that sounds simple, but it felt bigger than I expected.

I had always assumed confidence came first. You become confident, and then you wear the lingerie. You become confident, and then you take the pictures. You become confident, and then you stop hiding. But maybe sometimes you do the wildly uncomfortable thing first, and confidence catches up with you once you’re already there. And, to note, I wasn’t suddenly fearless during the shoot. My brain still tried to remind me of everything I normally dislike about myself.

The difference this time? I kept going. I didn’t wait until I felt completely comfortable because, if we’re being honest, I might have been waiting forever. How many things have I delayed because I thought I needed to become a different version of myself first? I’ll do that when I lose weight, when I’m stronger, happier, less anxious, more confident, more put together. I have spent a lot of time waiting to feel ready, and I’m starting to realize “ready” might be a scam. Sometimes you just go.

You show up nervous and uncomfortable, with the same body, the same brain, and the same insecurities you had yesterday, and you see what happens. I didn’t leave my boudoir shoot magically healed. I still have bad body image days, and I still know exactly which angles I prefer because I am a millennial woman who survived the early 2000s. Seriously, haven’t we millennials been through enough? But I have started to see myself differently.

More importantly, I let myself be seen. Not after I changed. Not once I lost the weight, toned the thing, or finally decided I was “good enough”. I don’t think I realized how often I was waiting for a better version of myself to arrive before I allowed the current version of me to fully participate in my own life. The current version is the one who is here, though, and she’s the one who gets to do the things. So yes, I did a boudoir shoot. I was terrified. I was awkward. I had absolutely no idea what to do with my face half the time, and I’m fairly certain I discovered muscles I didn’t know existed. And I would absolutely do it again, but not because I finally love every single inch of my body.

Because I’m starting to learn I don’t have to.
